children.translated_text: <s>Pilindavatsa</s> addressed the goddess of the <s>Gaṅgā</s> as '<s>vṛṣalī</s>' (low-caste woman), and so forth. Moreover, complete knowledge of the <s>Vinaya</s> is by no means [easily] accomplished, because of its difficulty. Like the impossibility of <s>Sthūla</s> and <s>Kumārī</s> remaining together on one ground, and because of the abundance of obstacles in endeavors. Since this subject matter is varied.] (That is to say,) if, venerable one, a <s>traividya</s> (one learned in three knowledges) of three years who has abandoned the three defilements (<s>trimala</s>) is not endowed with the five <s>dharmas</s>, should he too travel the countryside without reliance? 'No, <s>Upāli</s>,' it is said. And he should guard what pertains to the <s>Vinaya</s>; let him keep far away from that [transgression], for the purpose of attaining the state of being protected. For the purpose of avoiding that conduct which would cause others' displeasure. Even one who has accomplished his purpose in the trainings (<s>śikṣā</s>) should be respectful here, for the purpose of generating reverence. And for the sake of the continued existence of the Teaching (<s>śāsana</s>), transgression of what is well-established proceeds [to destruction]. When there is some transgression, the destruction of the Teaching comes about otherwise. Therefore, just as for another there is no permission here [to go without reliance], so too for the <s>traividya</s>. This concludes the section on reliance (<s>niśraya</s>).

body.translated_text: (70) One should not do anything requiring dependence without consulting one's shelter-giver (<s>niśraya</s>). 'Not consulting' means 'not asking'; the meaning is: one should not do anything without asking. Since one engaged in consultation regarding duties may perform certain duties without asking, the <s>Bhagavān</s> has stated [exceptions]: (71) Except for going to urinate or defecate, disposing of the tooth-stick, and paying homage to the <s>caitya</s> (shrine) together with its courtyard in the <s>vihāra</s> (monastery). That which is pervaded by the inner activities such as scratching etc. is the <s>caitya</s> courtyard; there the courtyard is appropriate. 'Together with the courtyard' (<s>sopavicāra</s>); therein is the <s>caitya</s>; paying homage to it. (72) Going up to forty-nine <s>vyāma</s>-lengths (fathoms) from the <s>vihāra</s>. 'Except' continues [from above]. 'Forty-nine' — the meaning is 'up to the limit of forty-nine <s>vyāma</s>-lengths.' Where the <s>vihāra</s> has a moat, a wall, or other enclosure, that is understood as the boundary of the <s>vihāra</s>. When there are multiple walls etc., the outermost one [is the boundary]. Therefore, the outer side of that [wall] is the limit of this measure. Where there is no courtyard, the <s>vihāra</s> wall itself is the boundary. What lies beyond this, where the previously mentioned courtyard is located — the <s>caitya</s> situated there need not be saluted; this is established here. This permission is for [one going about as] a stroll. Furthermore, regarding paying homage to the <s>caitya</s>: what should be done? — One should not go for that purpose without asking. But if one has gone for a stroll, one should pay homage. This duty is twofold: that which is an initiative and that which is a paying of respect. Of these, the prohibition applies only to what is an initiative; what is a paying of respect is not to be prohibited. Without asking, one should not address, not converse, not exchange greetings, not give a reply, not with a hand wet with water or anointed touch the feet or face or heart etc., not wipe one's hands etc. with water, not dust off garments covered with dust, etc. — lest an offense of a laughable nature occur.

children.translated_text: (106) For that purpose — one who does not possess that [quality], having been brought up to the stage of having attained <s>upāsaka</s> (lay-follower) status, the <s>saṃgha</s> should make him undergo probation (<s>parivāsa</s>) for four months, having granted the probation by a formal act. 'For that purpose' means for the purpose of having his mind won over; 'one who does not possess that' means one whose mind has not been won over. 'That' (<s>tad</s>) refers to the non-Buddhist sectarian. 'Having been brought up to the stage of attaining <s>upāsaka</s> status' means having performed the procedure up to the attainment of <s>upāsaka</s> status. Thus, by a formal act with a motion and three proclamations (<s>jñapticaturtha karma</s>), the <s>saṃgha</s>, having granted the probation of four months, should make [him] undergo probation. Regarding the grant of probation: (107) His food [should come] from the <s>saṃgha</s>. (108) His robes [should come] from the preceptor (<s>upādhyāya</s>). (109) The agency of the action and the giving [of the probation belongs to the act-performer]. (110) 'Are you fifteen years old?' — [the preceptor] should ask one who has approached for the purpose of ordination. The preceptor [should ask]. (111) One who is less [than fifteen years] and incapable — in the case of <s>Kākoḍḍāyana</s> — or one who is capable but [only] seven years old — they should not ordain [such ones]. These two should not be ordained: one who is incapable and less than fifteen years of age, and one who is capable but [only] seven years of age. They should not ordain. Why the plural? For the purpose of including [the idea that] the announcer, knowing 'this one is impure,' should not announce; the <s>saṃgha</s> should not authorize; the one who confers novice status should not confer novice status. (112) One should not maintain more than one novice-trainee (<s>śramaṇoddeśa</s>) at a time. In order to refute [the view] that the prohibition against maintaining a second novice-trainee also means a prohibition against ordaining a second [person], he says: (113) If there is displeasure with ordaining [them] together at once, [the preceptor] should fully ordain the one in excess of the ordination [candidate]. When two have come with the resolve 'We two shall be ordained at the same place,' if there is displeasure — that is, reluctance — about ordaining [them] together at once, then having ordained both, the one in excess of the first should be fully ordained. (114) If [one of the two] is under age, [the preceptor] should entrust him to another for the purpose of dependence (<s>upaniśraya</s>). If he is under twenty years of age, then he should be entrusted to another <s>bhikṣu</s> for the purpose of dependence. The one to whom he has been entrusted for the purpose of dependence: (115) That [other bhikṣu] should not take him away. The one by whom [the candidate] was entrusted — he (116) should fully ordain [him], without forcibly taking [him] from the one who does not give [him back]. Since the giving for dependence on another is for the sake of propriety, not by way of [permanent] consignment — therefore there should be no taking away. (117) <s>Kṛt</s>: a slave (<s>dāsa</s>). By this designation <s>kṛt</s>, [the formula] 'are you not...' and so forth [applies to] one connected with [the status of] slave. Therefore, in this instance of the designation [<s>kṛt</s>], the additional [category] that is accepted is converted according to its meaning and placed in its proper position. And the sentence known here is: 'Are you not a slave?' — [the preceptor] should ask one who has approached for the purpose of ordination; and the ordainers should not ordain or fully ordain a slave. (118) 'Removing [the word "are"] (<s>asi</s>), [ask]: Do you owe anything to anyone, small or great?' '<s>Vyasi</s>' means 'devoid of <s>asi</s>.' The word <s>kṛt</s> should be stated excluding the word '<s>asi</s>' — this is the meaning. And in place of '<s>asi</s>' (you are), '<s>te</s>' (to you) should be said; then this sentence [reads]: 'Do you not owe anything to anyone, small or great?' — [the preceptor] should ask one who has approached for the purpose of ordination; and the ordainers — they should not ordain or fully ordain one who is in debt — from the formula. children.translated_text: The qualification 'not indebted' should be understood as a specific [requirement]. // (119) One whose parents are living (<s>jīvatpitṛka</s>), who has not been permitted by them, who is from a nearby region and is seeking ordination (<s>pravrajyā</s>), should be kept [waiting] for seven days. One whose parents are alive is called <s>jīvatpitṛka</s>. 'By them' means by the mother and father. And from the word 'by them' (<s>tābhyām</s>), the word 'father' (<s>pitṛ</s>) here [includes] both mother and father. // (120) Even without being informed [by the parents], one from a distant region should be ordained in the <s>Saṃgha</s>. // 'Him' refers to one with living parents who has been permitted. For one who does not have living parents, or for one who has been permitted by mother and father, even not informing [the parents] is understood to be faultless. Or thus, the reading of the question regarding one with living parents: 'Venerable sir, for one whose mother and father have died or have gone to an animal birth — for his tonsure, the entire <s>Saṃgha</s> should be consulted' — 'This is not so, <s>Upālin</s>.' Why was the specification 'distant region' made? Because a certain householder's wife came and said to her son who had gone forth: 'Why have you gone forth among these thieving followers of the <s>Śākyaputra</s> (Son of the Śākyas)? Come, let us go.' He was seized by her and taken home. Thus, the danger here is the conduct [of taking him back] by theft. Yet in a distant region, there is no absence of this [danger], since even when the parents who remain in their own place hear of what has been done, it becomes a source of danger, and since it is possible for them to come and create danger even [from afar]. Therefore, [the sūtra] states 'even from a distant region.' // (121) It is fitting for the <s>Saṃgha</s> to give food to one seeking ordination. // 'Fitting' means this is not an absolute rule; it indicates that the <s>bhikṣus</s> should not be negligent [about this]. // (122) [Ask:] 'Have you been permitted by your mother and father?' — appending 'except for one from a distant region' at the end. // 'Have you been permitted' stands in place of 'Are you not?' The word 'except for one from a distant region' should be understood as additional to what was stated with 'kṛt' at the end. Thus the statement is: 'Have you been permitted by your mother and father?' From 'for the purpose of ordination' onward up to: 'one not permitted by mother and father should not be ordained or given full ordination, except for one from a distant region.' // (123) 'Are you ill?' — this should be asked of one who has approached for ordination. // 'For the purpose of ordination' is to be understood from context. // (124) Or: 'Do you have any illness?' // This is the basis for a variant reading. It shows that either of the two may be spoken. // (125) The ordainers (<s>upasaṃpādakas</s>) should [ask] specifically. // The connection is that 'should ask,' in its [plural] form 'should they ask,' carries over: 'There are indeed such bodily afflictions (<s>ābādhās</s>) in the bodies of men, namely: leprosy (<s>kuṣṭha</s>), tumor (<s>gaṇḍa</s>), and so forth' — with specific [diseases mentioned]. Not merely 'Are you ill?' // (126) One who is ill should not be ordained or given full ordination. // The plural is used because many [persons] are involved — the announcer, the ordainer, the novice, the candidate, and the <s>Saṃgha</s>. // (127) 'Kṛt' [applies to everything] before 'praṇihita.' // From '[one should] not [ordain one who has] accepted a mark of perversion (that was) established' — before that, throughout all [the sūtras], 'kṛt' should be understood as governing. All of those are connected with 'kṛt.' // (128) And [one should ask] 'there is no nature of regrowth in him.' // The 'and' (<s>ca</s>) connects the one prohibited here — the <s>nirmita</s> (magically created) and others — with [the sūtras] before 'praṇihita.' // (129) Expulsion of such a person who bears the marks [of ordination]. // 'Such a person' means one in whom there is no nature of regrowth. 'One bearing the marks' (<s>liṅgin</s>) means one who has gone forth or been fully ordained. // But for one who is a householder, dwelling among <s>bhikṣus</s>,

whether there is expulsion or not, depending on the purpose of traveling, of one who dwells [among them]. // Now those connected with 'kṛt' and so forth are specified: (130) <s>Nirmita</s> (a magically created being). // One should ask 'Are you a <s>nirmita</s>?' of one who has approached for the purpose of ordination, and the ordainers [should also ask]; one should not ordain or give full ordination to a <s>nirmita</s>. // 'There is no nature of regrowth in him; expulsion of such a person who bears the marks' — this should be applied similarly to <s>paṇḍakas</s> (eunuchs) and others elsewhere as well. // (131) <s>Paṇḍaka</s> (eunuch). // There is a fivefold [classification] of this. // 'Of this' means of the <s>paṇḍaka</s>. What are the five? // (132) By birth, by half-month, by contact-manifestation, by jealousy-manifestation, and one made so by calamity. // A <s>jāti-paṇḍaka</s> is one who is a <s>paṇḍaka</s> by birth — one who from birth is neither woman nor man. // 'By half-month' (<s>pakṣa</s>): one who is female in one half-month and male in the other — that is a <s>pakṣa-paṇḍaka</s>. A 'half-month' (<s>pakṣa</s>) is a fortnight. // 'By contact-manifestation' (<s>āsaktaprādurbhāva</s>): one in whom manifestation occurs when sexually approached by another — that is an <s>āsakta-paṇḍaka</s>. // 'By jealousy' (<s>īrṣyā</s>): one in whom manifestation occurs upon seeing a woman being sexually approached by another — that is an <s>īrṣyā-paṇḍaka</s>. // 'Made by calamity' (<s>āpatkṛt</s>): an <s>āpat-paṇḍaka</s> is one whose male organ has been destroyed by cutting or the like. // (133) For the last of these, expulsion when there is partaking of the defect. // 'For the last' means for the <s>āpat-paṇḍaka</s>. // He immediately partakes of the <s>paṇḍaka</s> defect; therefore he should be expelled, and not otherwise — this is the meaning. // (134) <s>Steya-saṃvāsika</s> (one who dwells by theft [of ordination]). // Its definition is stated: The truth [of steya-saṃvāsika status is established] when one knowingly [acknowledges] the non-performance of the prescribed procedure of full ordination, or the non-establishment [of ordination] even when the procedure was performed, in the experience of a second [saṃgha] act together with the <s>Saṃgha</s>. The 'prescribed procedure' of full ordination is the formal act beginning with the announcement (<s>jñapti</s>); 'knowing its non-performance' — or, even when the procedure was performed, [knowing] its non-establishment, because of a defect such as being under twenty years of age. The truth [of steya-saṃvāsika status lies] in the experience of a second act together with the <s>Saṃgha</s>. // Objection: But it was stated: 'Since, <s>Upālin</s>, two or three <s>poṣadha</s> (confession) ceremonies have been experienced together with properly constituted <s>bhikṣus</s> — to that extent one is a <s>steya-saṃvāsika</s>.' Then why was 'or three' not included in the sūtra? Because that statement does not establish an absolute rule; rather, it is a demonstration of the sequence. One who begins the sequence is disrupted [by the second occurrence]. Otherwise, 'or three' would be understood as a respite from the determination of 'two.' Thus this [distinction] is artificial and conventional, not established by the nature of things — and this follows. // And there is a textual difficulty here. In the narrative context, the very ground on which a <s>steya-saṃvāsika</s> should not be ordained or given full ordination would be the very ground on which he should be ordained or given full ordination — [to which] it is said: one who has experienced two or three <s>poṣadha</s> ceremonies should not be ordained or given full ordination; but one who has experienced a single <s>poṣadha</s> should be ordained and given full ordination. For otherwise, there is no definitive [basis], with the experience of two [being sufficient for] worthiness. // The reasoning, however, is that one who first engages [in this] is apprehensive; his falsity has not become his nature. But one who persists becomes fully absorbed in it. // Objection: Now, the term '<s>poṣadha</s>' was used [in the source]; why then is the experience of all <s>saṃgha</s> acts mentioned here without distinction? Reply: Because this is included in what pertains to the <s>saṃgha</s>'s congregation — since [participation in] the <s>poṣadha</s> and other acts equally [requires] being in the purview of the <s>saṃgha</s>. // Therefore, by way of illustration,

children.translated_text: ...the observance of <s>poṣadha</s> (fortnightly confession) is established. // In the procedure of inquiry into offenses when ordination (<s>upasaṃpad</s>) is incomplete, here too scriptural authority (<s>āgama</s>) applies. It is stated: 'By a formal act with a motion and three announcements (<s>jñapticaturtha</s>), for an unordained person in a <s>saṅgha</s> procedure, whether at <s>poṣadha</s> or at <s>pravāraṇā</s> (invitation ceremony), the experience of twelve persons [is relevant]; to this extent one becomes a <s>steyasaṃvāsaka</s> (one secretly living [in the <s>saṅgha</s>]).' Inasmuch as what is indicated by activities not to be performed by an unordained person — such as the announcement to the <s>saṅgha</s> of one seeking ordination — all this, being dependent on the entire <s>saṅgha</s>, belongs to the category of <s>saṅgha</s>-procedures. Therefore, the acceptance of formal procedures is also to be understood here: if, for one who has experienced the announcements of ordination, conferral of novice status, private instruction, purity, collection, and the announcement of <s>parivāsa</s> (probation) etc., the status of <s>steyasaṃvāsaka</s> is established. // (135) '<s>Tīrthikaprakrāntaka</s>' (one who has departed to non-Buddhist teachers). // For the purpose of explaining its nature — (136) 'For one whose ordination has been undertaken, [if he adopts] their views, setting aside this robe, [taking up] that banner, there [remaining] at sunrise — that is the reality.' // Thus it is stated. 'One whose ordination has been undertaken' means one who has ordination by undertaking it. 'Of their views' means in the views of the <s>tīrthikas</s> (non-Buddhist teachers); one established in these is 'one holding their views.' 'Setting aside this robe' means abandoning the garb of a <s>bhikṣu</s> of the <s>Sugata</s>. 'With that banner' means with the banner of the <s>tīrthika</s>. 'There' means in the state of the <s>tīrthika</s>. 'At sunrise, that is the reality' means the status of <s>tīrthikāvakrāntaka</s> (one who has entered a non-Buddhist order). // (137) Even if that [formal adoption of their views] is not done, it is like theft (<s>steya</s>). // Having cast off the garb of the <s>Tathāgata</s>, if one who desires [to join] the <s>tīrthikas</s>, concealing himself with the desired emblems, stays until sunrise — this is the adoption of the <s>Tathāgata</s>'s emblems, not the <s>tīrthika</s>'s views. This is 'that which is not done.' // Subsequently, if even without this being done, there is nevertheless a going over to the <s>tīrthikas</s>, then it is like theft — it is included within theft itself; therefore the meaning is that there are two kinds of experience. // (Thus) the status of <s>steyasaṃvāsaka</s> has been stated. // (138–145) One who has killed his mother. // One who has killed his father. // One who has killed an <s>arhat</s>. // A schismatic of the <s>saṅgha</s> (<s>saṃghabhedaka</s>). // One who, with a malicious mind, has drawn blood from the <s>Tathāgata</s>. // A defiler of a <s>bhikṣuṇī</s>. // One who has incurred any one of the four <s>pārājika</s> (defeats) [or not]. // One who has not accepted — the reversal of grounds is established as the non-performance of ordination and full ordination. // 'Reversal of grounds' means: the reversal of the grounds — such as quarrel, dispute, etc. — by which the desired procedure of reproof etc. takes place, [that is,] the absence of quarrel, dispute, etc. // The non-acceptance of what is established is the absence of the means [for ordination]. // (146) Ordination [requires] consent and a formal motion (<s>jñapti</s>). // Those who have not consented are unordained, since they are not fit for the status of being ordained; what is not consent for another purpose is consent — i.e., the function of consent. body.translated_text: (103) 'Are you not a non-Buddhist sectarian (<s>tīrthya</s>)?' — [the preceptor] should ask one who has approached for the purpose of ordination (<s>pravrajyā</s>), and the ordainers [should ask] also. 'Should ask' refers to the preceptor. 'Should ask' [in the plural] — when [the candidate] has been presented — the connection is with 'the ordainers.' The same question that is asked by the private instructor (<s>rahonuśāsaka</s>) [is asked] by the ordainers themselves, because he [the private instructor] is appointed by them. (104) One whose mind has not been won over (<s>anārādhitacitta</s>) — excepting a <s>Śākya</s> and a fire-worshipping ascetic (<s>āgneya jaṭila</s>) — they should not ordain or fully ordain a non-Buddhist sectarian. For the <s>Śākya</s> and fire-worshipping castes, certainly some affinity of disposition was observed: 'Surely, when these two practice, their practice will be genuine, not artificial.' Therefore it should be understood that this [exception] was permitted. And as for what was said: 'I grant to my kinsmen a kinsmen's concession,' therein the <s>Bhagavān</s> discerned that 'for those who do not regard themselves as kinsmen, genuine practice will occur,' and therefore the concession was given on account of kinship — thus it was stated. The 'fire-worshipper' (<s>āgneya</s>) here is one engaged in the practice of fire-tending; he should be understood as accepted because he is abiding in genuine purity of disposition, since for one truly of that nature, corruption of disposition is inconceivable. The word <s>kṛt</s> (a technical label) represents the exclusion from [the category] 'non-Buddhist sectarian' to 'one whose mind has not been won over' to 'non-Buddhist sectarian.' By the word [<s>kṛt</s>], excluding the initial word 'non-Buddhist sectarian,' and setting aside 'one whose mind has not been won over,' 'a <s>Śākya</s> and a fire-worshipping ascetic, a non-Buddhist sectarian' — and excluding from the word 'one whose mind has not been won over' to the word 'non-Buddhist sectarian' — what is stated beginning with 'are you not' should be understood as designated by [the label] <s>kṛt</s>. Wherever '<s>kṛt</s>' is stated, there [the formula] 'are you not [a...] — one should ask one who has approached for the purpose of ordination, and the ordainers should not ordain or fully ordain [such a one]' should be understood as having been declared. The passages marked <s>kṛt</s> [occur] hereafter in this very chapter on ordination (<s>pravrajyāvastu</s>) and in the minor rules (<s>kṣudraka</s>) pertaining to this topic. To determine at what point a non-Buddhist sectarian is to be called 'one whose mind has been won over,' he says: (105) When the merits of the [Three] Jewels (<s>ratna</s>) and the demerits of the non-Buddhist sectarians are truthfully proclaimed, remaining unshaken constitutes having one's mind won over (<s>ārādhitacittatā</s>). 'Does not become angry' (<s>akupya</s>) means unshaken; the state of being unshaken is 'unshakability' (<s>akupyatva</s>).

body.text: hastacchinā iti maṇibandhamudgṛhya yeṣāṃ hastāḥ chinnāḥ // pādacchinnā iti yeṣāṃ āgulphaṃ chedaḥ te pādacchinnāḥ // yesāṃ hastāṅgulayo nāgaphaṇasaḍṛśāḥ aṅgulīphaṇahastakāḥ / yeṣāṃ oṣṭhakadvayābhāvaḥ te anoṣṭhakāḥ // yesāṃ kāye citracihnāni te citrāṅgāḥ / hastādiṣu citritaḥ citrāṅgāḥ / avirataṃ sravanta iva ityādayaḥ // ativṛddhā iti śatavārṣikādayaḥ / atibālakā iti kākoḍḍāpane 'samarthaḥ asaptavarṣakaḥ // khañjā iti pādena khañjagamanāḥ // kāṇḍarika iti sakthipakṣa-gṛdhrasīvātena saṃdhvastagamanaḥ // kāṇaḥ ekākṣaḥ // kuṇiḥ yasya maṇibandhapakṣe cihnamātrahaste sati kiñcidapi karaṇe asamarthaḥ // galagaḍaḥ grīvā-gaṇḍikā yasya sa galagaṇḍaḥ // mūkaḥ vāgasamarthaḥ // pīṭhasarpi iti ādhārārthaṃ hastadvayaṃ pratiṣṭhāpya caturūpeṇa sarpati / dvitīyaḥ paryāyaḥ phakkaḥ ityapi / strīcchinnaḥ // strīṇāṃ utkaṭasevanayā kṣatavīryaḥ, yasya kāyaḥ asukhaḥ strīcchinnaḥ // tathaiva akṣamabhāradhāraṇāt (

body.text: (149) kṛt* rājabhaṭaḥ / ananujñātaṃ rājñā adūradeśikam // ityasmin 'na rājabhaṭo 'si' iti pravrajyātvamupasaṃkrāntaṃ praṣṭavyam / upasaṃpādakairapi rājabhaṭaḥ rājñā 'nanujñātaḥ adūradeśikaḥ na pravrājayitavyaḥ upasaṃpādayitavyaśca iti // yaḥ pravrajyāvastumārgaṃ gṛhṇāti tasmai etena upadeṣṭavyam / yo rājā vā tadvijitaḥ prabhurvā, tena yena kenacit mārṣeṃṇa vā tatpadasaṃbaddhaḥ sa atra adūradeśikaḥ // (150) kṛt* cauro prajñātaḥ // iti rājñā nā 'nanujñātaḥ adūradeśikaḥ ityetannirākaraṇārtha punaḥ kṛcchabdaḥ / cauro] nāsi dhvajabaddhakaḥ iti pravrajyārthaṃ upasaṃkrāntaḥ pṛcchet upasaṃpādakāśca, na cauraṃ dhvajabaddhakaṃ pravrājayeyuḥ upasaṃpādayeyurvā / ityetāvatā evamapi atra vidhānasya bhāvaḥ // prajñātacauro dhvajabaddhakaḥ / yatra yasya na prajñāyamānatvaṃ na tatra tasya dhvajabaddhakatvam // (151) na rathakāra-[carmakāra]-caṇḍāla-pukkala-tadvidhān pravrājayet // rathakāraḥ carmakāraḥ, tadvidhān iti abhokṣya-[anu]śrāmaṇeratvaśikṣamāṇatva-upasaṃpādanā 'narhatvaṃ rathakārādīnāṃ apravrājane nimittam / tasmāt āsāṃ api etadakaraṇīyatvasya pratipādanam // (152) nidarśanaṃ hastacchinnādayaḥ // yadetad pravrajyāvastuni hastacchinna-pādacchinnetyādi uktaṃ nidarśanaṃ tadveditavyam, na parisaṃkhyānam / yeṣāmetad nidarśanaṃ tānīdānīṃ upanyasyati-
body.translated_text: (149) 'A royal soldier (<s>rājabhaṭa</s>); one from a nearby region not permitted by the king.' // In this [context], the question 'Are you not a royal soldier?' should be asked of one who has come seeking ordination (<s>pravrajyā</s>). Also, those performing the ordination should not ordain or grant full ordination to a royal soldier not permitted by the king, [nor to] one from a nearby region. // Whoever takes up the path of the <s>Pravrajyāvastu</s>, to him this should be taught: whoever is a king, or one under his dominion, or a lord, or anyone connected with that position through some lineage — he is here [designated as] 'one from a nearby region.' // (150) 'A thief who is known.' // The word '<s>kṛt</s>' is repeated for the purpose of negating [the applicability of] 'not permitted by the king, from a nearby region.' [The question] 'Are you not a thief or one sentenced [to punishment]?' should be asked of one who has come seeking ordination; and those performing the ordination should not ordain or grant full ordination to a thief or one sentenced. To this extent, the existence of a rule in this regard [is established]. // A known thief is one sentenced [to punishment]. Where one is not known [as a thief], there is no status of being sentenced. // (151) One should not ordain a <s>rathakāra</s> (chariot-maker), <s>carmakāra</s> (leather-worker), <s>caṇḍāla</s> (outcaste), <s>pukkala</s> (a low-caste person), or those of similar kind. // '<s>Rathakāra</s>' means leather-worker. 'Those of similar kind' means: the unsuitability for the status of one with whom food may not be shared, of a novice (<s>śrāmaṇera</s>), of a probationer (<s>śikṣamāṇā</s>), and for full ordination — this is the ground for not ordaining <s>rathakāras</s> and others. Therefore, for these [categories] too, the non-performance of this [ordination] is taught. // (152) The examples are those beginning with 'hand-cut.' // That which was stated in the <s>Pravrajyāvastu</s> — 'hand-cut, foot-cut,' and so forth — should be understood as illustrative, not as an exhaustive enumeration. Those for whom this is illustrative — those he now presents:

body.text: tamiti hastacchinnāḥ pādachinnāḥ ityevamādikaṃ pratikṣepaṃ evaṃ vidhānāmapi pradhārayet ityarthaḥ // haridrā iva raktā keśā yeṣāṃ te haridrakeśāḥ / siṃhakeśā harikeśā // nīlyā iva raktā keśā yeṣāṃ haritakeśāḥ // janmanā eva śuklā keṣā yesāṃ te avadātakeśā, na tu palitinaḥ // hastina iva yeṣāṃ keśā te nāgakeśā // tāmrabhājanamiva ślakṣṇaṃ vigatakeśaśiro yeṣāṃ te akeśakāḥ // yasya śirasi tasraḥ catasro vā sthūlavalayaḥ, yābhiḥ nimnonnataṃ lakṣyate, sa ghāṭośiraḥ // yeṣāṃ piśvitamiva śarīraṃ vaipulavataḥ // [pṛthagvat] saṃkṣiptakaṃ te vipātakāḥ // yasya atisaṃkṣipte vartulākṣiṇī te saṃcūrṇākṣāḥ [=cullākṣāḥ?] // śiraso 'ntaḥ praviṣṭatvāt skandhasthāne akṣiṇī yasya asau skandhākṣaḥ // lāṅgūlaṃ yasya prasravakaraṇaṃ ta[d yasya chinnaṃ] sa lāṅgūlachinnaḥ // yesāṃ svalpenā 'pi vyāpāreṇa viśiṣṭaśramotpattiḥ te 'tikilāsinaḥ, klamasyaitadabhidhānam // caturbhiśca chavivarṇaiḥ iti nīlapatīlohitāvadātaiḥ (ninditarūpāḥ) / ye evaṃvidhā varṇaviśeṣāḥ teṣāṃ eva pratikṣepaḥ na tu ye devānāmiva praśasyarūpāḥ // evaṃ tāvat evaṃvidhānāṃ pravrājanādikaṃ pratikṣiptam / pravrajitopasaṃpannānāmeṣāṃ api saṃgraho na ityu padarśanāya āha // (153) na jātikāyaduṣṭaṃ pravrajitaṃ upasthāpayet // rathakārādikaṃ abhokṣyaṃ jātiduṣṭam / hastacchinnādikaṃ varṇataḥ saṃsthānato vā kāyena (

) duṣṭaṃ / nopasthāpayet, vāsasthāne 'pi antardāne, na anuparivāritvena ca, na kevalaṃ niśrayadāne / tathā ca bhikṣuṇā parṣad dūṣakaparṣad, na upasthāpayitavyā, upasthāpayati sātisāro bhavati / ityuktvā kiyatā parṣad dū[ṣakā] parṣad iti vaktavyā? / jātito varṇasaṃsthānena ca // kathaṃ jātitaḥ? / rathakāracaṇḍālapukkasakulāt // kathaṃ varṇasaṃsthānataḥ? haridrakeśā ityādyatroktam // (154) yujyate naikasyopādhyāyasya ekena vacasā upasaṃpādanaṃ ātrayāt / anekasyeti dviprabhṛteḥ / eka upādhyāyaḥ asyeti ekopādhyāyaḥ, tasya / ekena vacasā iti ekaprajñaptyā / ki yato 'nekasya ityāha / ātrayāt* tribhyo yāvat yujyate, na pareṇa ityarthaḥ
// 'na gaṇo gaṇasya karmāṇi karoti' ityāgamāt // kecit - aṃgīkṛtopādhyāyabhedaṃ atra granthaṃ kurvate - 'labhyaṃ bhadanta ekakāle ekakṣaṇe ekena karmakārakeṇa ekayā jñaptyā dvābhyāṃ karmāṇi kartum? kṛtāni ca vaktavyāni? na ca saṃghaḥ tena sā tisāro bhavati'? - 'labhyaṃ upālin sa cet karmakārako bhikṣuḥ pratibalo bhavati / upādhyāyānāṃ nāmaparikīrtanaṃ kartuṃ upasaṃpatprekṣāṇāṃ ca jñaptiṃ ca na hāpayati karma ca karoti' ityādi // ārya-upālino dāsakaḥ pālakaśca śrāmaṇerakau sapremakau gatau, anyonyānurakṣayā 'yugapat nopasaṃpādyau, [tasmāt pṛthak] dvau nopasaṃpadyate // etannidānaṃ ekopādhyāyasya anekasya upasaṃpādanānujñāne, asmānnidānāt ekopādhyāyasya anekasyāṅgīkaraṇaṃ atra nidānāt dṛśyate / ityevaṃ aṅgīkṛtaṃ na caitaṃ prayujyate // (155) ābhāvaḥ tulyasamayānāṃ parasparaṃ sāmocīkaraṇasya // ekakāle ekakarmavācanopasaṃpāditānāṃ, pṛthagvā upasaṃpannānāṃ, yeṣāṃ tulyasamayaḥ tesāṃ sāmīcīkaraṇasya parasparaṃ abhāvaḥ / sāmīcī vandanā // (156) saṃprāpte prāthamyam // tulyasamayānāṃ lābhakarmādānoddeśādi sthānaṃ, yaḥ prathamaṃ saṃprāptaḥ 'yathāgatikayā lābho grahītavyaḥ' iti vacanāt tasya lābhagrahaṇe prāthamyam // karmādāne yaḥ paścādāgataḥ tena pūrvakarma kartavyam paścādāgataḥ karmādāne prathamaṃ iti vacanāt / prathamaṃ kāryatādi ayamarthaḥ / lābhagrahaṇe prathamaṃ sthānaṃ saṃprāpte prāthamyam, karmādānakaraṇe pañcātsthānaṃ saṃprāpte prāthamyamiti // (157) na dvyaṅgulādūrdhvaṃ āraṇyakaḥ keśān dhārayet // (158) naitad arvāktvāt grāmāntikaḥ // arvāgbhāvaḥ arvāktvam / etasya dvyaṅgulasya arvāgbhāvāt ūrdhvaṃ dvyarghāṅgula pramāṇatā saṃprāptā / yāvanna dhārayitavyā ityatra jñānaṃ bhava[tīti veditavyam / grantho ']tra - āraṇyakena bhikṣuṇā dvyaṅgulā bālā dhārayitavyā, arvāk grāmāntikena iti // kecit - 'dvyaṅgulāvartā' iti dvyaṅgulasthāne adhīyate / yadyasya pāṭhasya dvyaṅgulapramāṇa āvarto yeṣāṃ ityarthaḥ, anarthāntaratvaṃ pūrvakātpāṭhāt // atha dvyaṅgulasya āvarta ityayuktatā / liṅgāntardhānabhūtatvāt iyato (
children.translated_text: one who is corrupted — one should not admit [him], not even to the dwelling-place for internal donations, nor as an attendant, and not merely [restrict the prohibition] to the giving of shelter. And thus: 'A <s>bhikṣu</s> should not admit an assembly-defiling assembly; if he admits [such], he commits a transgression (<s>sātisāra</s>).' Having said this, to what extent is an assembly to be called 'assembly-defiling'? By birth, and by color and physical form. How by birth? From the family of a chariot-maker (<s>rathakāra</s>), outcaste (<s>caṇḍāla</s>), or <s>pukkasa</s>. How by color and physical form? 'Turmeric-haired' and so forth is stated here. (154) It is proper that one preceptor can fully ordain more than one [candidate] with a single proclamation — up to three. 'More than one' means two or more. 'One preceptor' (<s>ekopādhyāya</s>) means one who has one preceptor — of that [preceptor]. 'With a single proclamation' means with a single <s>jñapti</s> (formal motion). Up to how many? — He says: 'up to three' (<s>ātrayāt</s>) — it is proper up to three, not beyond — this is the meaning. From the scripture: 'A group does not perform the formal acts of [another] group.' Some construct the text here with the variant regarding the acceptance of a differentiated preceptor: 'Is it proper, <s>Bhadanta</s>, that at one time, at one moment, by one act-performer, with one <s>jñapti</s>, formal acts be performed for two? And [can they] be declared as performed? And the <s>saṃgha</s> does not thereby commit a transgression?' — 'It is proper, <s>Upālin</s>, if the act-performing <s>bhikṣu</s> is capable of making the proclamation of the preceptors' names, and of those seeking full ordination, and does not omit the <s>jñapti</s>, and performs the act' — and so forth. The venerable <s>Upāli</s>'s [novices] <s>Dāsaka</s> and <s>Pālaka</s>, being novices (<s>śrāmaṇera</s>) who were fond of each other, had gone [together]; because of their mutual attachment, they could not be fully ordained simultaneously — therefore two cannot be fully ordained [at once under the same preceptor]. This is the origin of the permission for a single preceptor to fully ordain more than one; from this origin, the acceptance of more than one by a single preceptor is seen here — it is thus accepted, but this [particular case] does not apply. (155) There is an absence of mutual salutation (<s>sāmīcīkaraṇa</s>) among those who are of equal standing. For those fully ordained at the same time by the same <s>karmavācanā</s> (formal proclamation), or ordained separately but having equal standing — among those whose standing is equal, there is no mutual salutation. '<s>Sāmīcī</s>' means prostration (<s>vandanā</s>). (156) For one who has arrived [first], there is priority. Among those of equal standing, in matters of receiving gains, performing acts, donations, recitation assignments, and so forth, the one who arrived first — from the statement 'gains should be received in order of arrival' — has priority in receiving gains. In performing acts, the one who arrived later should perform the prior act — from the statement 'the one who arrived later has priority in performing acts.' Priority means being first in obligation and so forth — this is the meaning. In receiving gains, the first position [goes to] the one who arrived first; in performing acts, the fifth position [goes to] the one who arrived first — [this is] priority. (157) A forest-dwelling monk (<s>āraṇyaka</s>) should not keep hair longer than two finger-widths (<s>aṅgula</s>). (158) This [limit] does not [apply] to a village-dwelling monk, because it is less. 'Lessness' (<s>arvāktva</s>) means being less. Because of being less than this two finger-widths, the standard of two-and-a-half finger-widths is reached — [this is the limit] beyond which [hair] should not be kept — this should be understood as the knowledge [conveyed] here. The text here is: 'A forest-dwelling <s>bhikṣu</s> should keep hair of two finger-widths; less [than that limit applies] for a village-dwelling monk.' Some read '<s>dvyaṅgulāvarta</s>' (two-finger-width curls) in place of 'two finger-widths.' If the meaning of this reading is 'those whose curls are of the measure of two finger-widths,' then there is no difference in meaning from the previous reading. But 'a curl of two finger-widths' would be inappropriate, because of being [only] the amount for concealing the sexual characteristics.

children.translated_text: [This is due to] its length, and because the training rule was established in connection with the causal fault, and because the occurrence of that fault remains in the same condition. Since the measure exceeds five finger-breadths, and because from the prescription of tonsure etc. at the time of ordination (<s>pravrajyā</s>), tonsure etc. is reasonably required to be performed also subsequently—therefore [this rule] is placed here. (159-162) One should not cut curly hair (<s>golomaka</s>). Except around a wound. One should not have a topknot (<s>cūḍā</s>) made. One should not have body-hair removal done in the private area (<s>saṃbādha-pradeśa</s>). 'One should not have done' is the continuation; the 'private area' means the genital region. (163) One may have it done on account of a wound, when [it is] not healed; otherwise, having consulted learned elder monks (<s>sthavira</s>). 'When not healed, otherwise' means—the Blessed One said: 'It should be cleansed with five astringents (<s>kaṣāya</s>). Afterwards, if health is not restored, having consulted <s>bhikṣus</s> who are bearers of the <s>Sūtra</s>, the <s>Vinaya</s>, and the <s>Mātṛkā</s>, one may have the hair in the private area shaved'—this is the [relevant] text. There, this is an illustration: since the cleansing procedure is appropriate, other modes of treatment are also permissible; having consulted elder monks, one may have body-hair removal done in the private area on account of a wound or on account of [harmful] creatures. According to others, this is the text: that which is done with the knowledge of those who are prominent—this is the consultation. Prominence among the two elders is by virtue of moral conduct and by knowledge of <s>Dharma</s> and <s>Vinaya</s>; both of these are encompassed and understood in the consultation. The mention of being a bearer of the <s>Piṭaka</s> constitutes 'knowledge.' 'On account of creatures' here is appropriately understood as referring to creatures in the wound, not to lice etc. And this is not taken as being subsumed under 'on account of a wound' alone. (164) One should not have the leg-hair (<s>aṅganāḍī</s>) [shaved] even for that reason. 'Not for that reason' means not on account of a wound. Shaving the shin is [what is meant by] '<s>aṅganāḍī</s>.' (165) Nor elsewhere on the body. On the body other than the private area and the legs—from the neck downward, whatever pertains to bodily practice—there is this prohibition of body-hair removal. Therefore, by this there is no prohibition of the requirement [to shave] head-hair and facial hair. The understanding is based on what is well known: there was no statement [prohibiting] the pulling out of nose hair. The text in the <s>Mātṛkā</s> is: 'Setting aside head-hair and facial hair, body hair on other limbs and parts of limbs should not be pulled out. Whoever pulls it out commits a <s>duṣkṛta</s> (wrongdoing) offense.' (166-168) One may use a razor-holder or a nail-cutter or a carpenter's adze. One should not polish these. One may use a scraper for removing dirt. One should not shave head-hair and facial hair with the robe. 'Robe' here is appropriately understood as the upper robe (<s>prāvaraṇa</s>), not the inner garment (<s>antarvāsa</s>). And for all, not with the saṃghāṭī or the upper robe (<s>uttarāsaṃga</s>) alone. Here, a different upper garment that has been used is appropriate. This is because the reason for the prohibition is established here. (169) One should keep a hair-receptacle (<s>keśapratigrahaṇa</s>). The 'hair-receptacle' is a robe [used for that purpose], whose use is precisely for that purpose. 'By which hairs are received'—this is the etymology. Why is it [called] a 'robe'? Because of the statement in the formula of designation (<s>adhiṣṭhāna</s>): 'The robe is the hair-receptacle, [this is] the designation.' But how is it known that it is for covering, and not for the actual shaving of hair there? Because in its absence, the <s>saṃkakṣikā</s> (shoulder-cloth) is mentioned. For shaving hair with the <s>saṃkakṣikā</s> is not prohibited. (170) In [its] absence,

with the <s>saṃkakṣikā</s> (shoulder-cloth). In the absence of the robe [serving as] hair-receptacle, one should shave head-hair and facial hair covered by the <s>saṃkakṣikā</s>. (171) Not on a mat. That is, one should not shave head-hair and facial hair [on a mat]. In the preliminary narratives (<s>nidāna</s>) too, the text ends with 'first, nail-cutting.' (172) Not where joint-sweepings fall. This pertains to the monastery regulations. (173-174) One may shave in an upper room etc. when aged or ill, and in wind, heat, and rain. One should clean that area. Cleaning means making it free of hair and free of water; it should be done in whatever way it is accomplished. (175) In a mixed [area], removal of children [is required]. The meaning is: in an area that is being cleaned. (176) Likewise for nail-cutting. This is an extension [of the rules] from 'not on a mat' etc. When a hair-receptacle is made to hold firmly, it is [effectively] placed on the ground. Therefore here, cutting where joint-sweepings fall—this is either already passed over, or the ground should be cleaned. In the shaving of head-hair and facial hair, the impossibility of this avoidance should be understood. (177) An undesignated <s>bhikṣuṇī</s> (nun) who has not overcome passion should not have her hair cut by a man. 'This' refers to a <s>bhikṣuṇī</s>; 'who has not overcome passion'—the text says 'there is no offense if she has overcome passion.' 'Should have cut' is an expression for tonsure as well. Now, <s>Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī</s>, together with five hundred <s>Śākyāyanī</s> women, having themselves cut their hair and donned saffron robes—since the cutting of hair that was mentioned is referred to as tonsure by the expression 'Just so, <s>Gautamī</s>, you are beautiful with a shaved head'; because the hair was long, this statement has a [specific] reason regarding another's tonsure. The practice otherwise is: a <s>bhikṣuṇī</s> who has not overcome passion, not designated by [another] <s>bhikṣuṇī</s>, should not have her hair cut by a man—this is the meaning. (178) The designating nun should instruct the one who is becoming passionate: 'Establish mindfulness—what essence is there in this body?' 'The one who is becoming passionate' refers to that <s>bhikṣuṇī</s> [being affected] by the barber. (179) [She should establish] the perception of mother, sister, or daughter regarding the barber. The designating nun should instruct the one becoming passionate: 'Establish the perception of [him as] mother etc.' (180) One should bathe when this is done. 'This' refers to the shaving of head-hair and facial hair. (181) Or the fivefold purification (<s>śauca</s>). The word 'or' is for the purpose of adopting an alternative practice. Even when water is available, this is permitted: 'A <s>bhikṣu</s> should keep a hair-receptacle, or should bathe, or at minimum should wash the hands and feet'—this is the text. (182) One should not bathe naked. Complete non-nakedness is when the three zones (<s>trimaṇḍala</s>) are covered. As long as the [area of] body-hair and the private parts are covered by the three-zone covering, so long is everything else not to be removed by virtue of being covered—this should be understood here by implication. (183) A <s>bhikṣuṇī</s> should not bathe at a men's bathing place; nor at a women's bathing place with powder. At a men's bathing place, bathing itself is prohibited for a <s>bhikṣuṇī</s>. But at a women's bathing place, [the prohibition is only] with mung-bean powder etc., while mere [partial] bathing is not prohibited. 'The group of twelve [nuns] bathe at a women's bathing place, behave frivolously toward the householders' wives who are bathing, and throw mung-bean powder etc. The Blessed One said: A <s>bhikṣuṇī</s> should not bathe at a women's bathing place with powder'—this is the text. (184) It is permitted

pratigupte pradeśe snānamiti // sarve na traicīvarikā eva / [atra granthaḥ] - apareṣāṃ snātraśāṭakasya prāptirnāsti, bhagavānāha - taiḥ patrāṇi purataḥ pṛṣṭhataśca datvā pratigupte pradeśe snātavyamiti aviśeṣeṇa etadabhihitam // (195) mocanena saktasya prāṇinaḥ apagatiḥ // ekapuṭāt atyāsaktiḥ dvipuṭe prāṇakānāmiti ataḥ pratipattiḥ / nāsya śāṭake dvipuṭatvasya abhāvaḥ / tasmāt nānena saprāṇake 'mbhasi snātavyamityatra sthitaṃ veditavyam // (196) udakabhrame (
children.translated_text: ) Powder perfumed with fragrance, made from mung beans and the like — all [monks] have the right [to use] this. (185-186) Its acceptance; and [acceptance] of that which is infused with medicine, by the sick. The continuation is '[it is] appropriate' [from a preceding aphorism]. (187) A nun (<s>bhikṣuṇī</s>) should not sprinkle powder on a woman. At bathing time and at other times as well — since no particular distinction is accepted, the rule [applies at all times]. It is stated in connection with avoiding nudity. (188) One should not climb a ladder with the lower garment's front and back hem untied at the bottom. The meaning is: [the hem] of the lower garment whose front and back lower edge — the edge that is at the bottom — is untied. This is for the avoidance of exposure of the undergarment (<s>kaupīna</s>). And even when climbing trees etc., there is the possibility of the undergarment being seen. Therefore, the mention of 'ladder' here should be understood as illustrative. In an emergency climb for the purpose of remedy — if the very tying of the garment [causes] hindrance to climbing, then its [proper wearing] should be maintained. If not, then one should proceed by the permission for climbing trees. (189) At other times, one should not be in that state. The meaning is: at times other than climbing a ladder, one should not have the front and back lower hem of the garment untied [but should remain properly dressed]. The undergarment facing inward — the avoidance of exposure of that [private part] in this context is what is being stated. (190) One should not leave the face uncovered [while yawning]. The non-covering by cloth etc. of one whose face is uncovered — that non-covering one should not practice. The text here is: 'A <s>bhikṣu</s> who is yawning should cover his mouth with his hand.' Here, the hand stands as illustrative. And yawning — this is stated with reference to its voluntary restraint [being possible]. When one is unable [to restrain it], there is no fault in not covering. (191-192) One should keep a bathing cloth (<s>snātraśāṭaka</s>). Insects cling to a folded [garment]. 'Clinging' is what should be said; the prefix 'ā-' is used for completeness in the commentary gloss. This is a statement of the reason. Because insects cling to a folded garment, therefore one should not bathe in water containing living beings with such a garment — this is the meaning. (193) Even one who possesses only the triple robe (<s>traicīvarika</s>). The continuation is: 'should keep a bathing cloth.' The text here is: 'The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: A <s>bhikṣu</s> who possesses only the triple robe should keep a bathing cloth.' Some read 'it should be kept without formal designation' — that is proper. Having obtained a bathing cloth, if the intention has not been generated, since a forfeiture offense (<s>naiḥsargika</s>) would arise, this intention must certainly be generated here. And upon its generation, the necessity of mental designation arises here. Therefore, performing another [type of] designation is proper, since verbal [designation] is easy; from this very permission, it should be understood that this does not become a share of his requisites. (194) Having placed leaf-bowls in front and behind, one should bathe in a concealed place. Not all [monks] possess only the triple robe. [The text here is:] 'For others, a bathing cloth is not obtainable; the <s>Bhagavān</s> said: They should bathe in a concealed place, having placed leaf-bowls in front and behind.' This is stated without restriction. (195) The removal of a clinging insect by loosening. From a single fold, there is excessive clinging [by insects] in a double fold — hence the rule. It is not the case that the bathing cloth lacks the property of being double-folded. Therefore, the established [rule] is that one should not bathe with it in water containing living beings. children.translated_text: ) — in the monastery, this [bathing is done]. If this bathing is done in the monastery, it should be done only at the water-drain (<s>udakabhrama</s>), not elsewhere. (197) And the draining of liquid. The draining of liquid from foot-washing etc. should be done only at the water-drain, not elsewhere. (198-199) Construction of a bathhouse (<s>snātraśālikā</s>). Laying of bricks therein — in that bathhouse. (200) Making of the water-drain; cleaning of the drainage channel (<s>syandanikā</s>). The <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'The water-drain should be announced.' There is a drainage channel; the <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'It should be cleaned from time to time.' Moreover, 'one should bathe only at the water-drain' — for the purpose of summarizing this, he says: (201) When bathing is done at the drain, there is no arising [of blockage] of the drainage channel. '<s>Snāti</s>' means bathing. 'Drainage channel' — this is the explanation by means of the remedy. When bathing takes place at the drain, there is no need for [repairing] the drainage channel. But this is not a restriction that one must bathe only at the drain, since the bathhouse is meant for bathing. (202) One should not scrub the body with a brick (<s>iṣṭaka</s>) — the [body] other than the feet. The text is: 'A <s>bhikṣu</s> should not scrub the body with a brick.' 'Other' means the body other than the feet. But for the feet, there is no prohibition. (203) This is illustrative of sharp and acidic [substances]. What kind of substance is a brick? — he says: sharp [things] like blades etc., and acidic [things] like alkali (<s>śauṇaka</s>) etc., because they produce mental disturbance. The <s>Bhagavān</s> has prescribed: 'The body should not be scrubbed with a brick.' The <s>bhikṣus</s> scrub with a shell; the <s>Bhagavān</s> said: 'A polished shell (<s>muṇḍaśukti</s>) should be used' — thus the text. Here indeed, the prohibition of the [unpolished] shell is due to its sharpness. Therefore, the brick is [merely] illustrative. The body should not be scrubbed with any other sharp or acidic substance either. (204) Cleaning of the shell with fire. Its cleaning with fire is merely by heating. Otherwise, the shell would be destroyed. (205) A nun should not rub anything [of the body] with anything, from a fist-sized cloth-roll (<s>cailavartta</s>) [down]. 'Anything' refers to the body. A woman's body is delicate; even from [something] soft and smooth, agitation arises in it. Even with the most inferior [material], a woman's disturbance [arises] from this action — hence for nuns there is a complete prohibition. 'Something softer than a fist-[sized cloth]' means: having stated 'of fist-size,' the mention of the cloth-roll [follows]. (206) One should not put on robes (<s>cīvara</s>) while water likely [to damage them] has not been removed. This is for the purpose of avoiding the destruction of robes being put on. Therefore, 'one from whom the water has not been removed' is the meaning. For one who does not wish to wait for [the water to dry], the next two rules [apply]: (207-208) One should keep a body-wiper (<s>kāyaproñchana</s>). In its absence, having stood in the squatting posture (<s>utkuṭuka</s>) for a moment, one should wipe with the bathing cloth. Or, the duration for which wiping with the bathing cloth serves its purpose — for that much time there is sufficiency. 'A moment' here is indicative of that [duration]. Or 'a moment' designates a small [amount of time]. 'Having stood in the squatting posture' — thus the water quickly departs from the body, and this posture is also a concealed form. Therefore, the avoidance of exposure [of private parts] is what is relied upon here. (209-210) One should use a steam-bath (<s>jentāka</s>). Construction of a steam-bath enclosure (<s>karaṇḍaka</s>) on elevated ground is proper. A <s>karaṇḍaka</s> is a dwelling for the purpose of a steam-bath. On ground with raised gravel, in such an elevated place, the enclosure —

To show what should be done in the basket-work [structure] (<s>karaṇḍa</s>), he says: (211) For a window that is narrow on the outside, wide on the inside, and shaped like an ocean [i.e., shell-shaped], the opening [should be] in the middle. 'Here' means in the window. (213) And the provision of a goat-foot stick. The word 'and' serves to connect with 'here.' 'Door' means the door of the basket-work [structure]. (215) For the purpose of storing hot water, the making of a pigeon-ledge (<s>kapotamālā</s>) on the inner side. The 'pigeon-ledge' here is a shelf on which water-pots are placed. (216-217) On the ground of the fire-place, the laying of bricks. For keeping the fire from going out, banking [the coals] — that is, arranging them in a circular shape. (218) For that purpose, the holding of iron tongs. [This refers to] the bathhouse (<s>jentākaśālā</s>). (220) To prevent dizziness, the throwing into the fire of roasted barley flour (<s>saktū</s>) smeared with pungent oil. 'Fire-intoxication' (<s>agnimada</s>) is dizziness (<s>tamikā</s>). (221) For the removal of bad smell, the offering of incense. [This addresses] the bad smell created by the barley flour. Here, in the bathhouse, [one uses] the under-arm ball as a seat; [the rule] that it should not [be used merely] for comfort as a seat — this is the permission [granted] for it. (224) The spreading of grass on the ground, moist — either naturally damp or dampened by sprinkling. Therein, 'naturally' means wetness that is inherent by nature; in its absence, wetness [achieved] by sprinkling should be relied upon — the purpose here is to prevent burning. children.translated_text: an unknown [person] who has come here — [the doorkeeper] should question [him] for the purpose of ascertaining [his identity]. The placement of a doorkeeper for this purpose, and also for preventing entry of a <s>bhikṣu</s> [who is disqualified]. 'At midday' means 'I am one other than yourselves' — with this implication [the unknown person enters]. 'One who has come here' means one who has come to the bathhouse (<s>jentāka</s>). 'Is this a <s>bhikṣu</s> or an <s>Ājīvika</s> and so forth?' — [the doorkeeper] should question for the purpose of ascertaining. 'The placement of a doorkeeper for this purpose' means: for the purpose of ascertaining the identity of an unknown person arriving at midday, and also for preventing entry — this is the meaning. 'By questioning, this [person] who is not one of ours is known' — of what sort should the doorkeeper be? — He says: 'a <s>bhikṣu</s>.' This is merely illustrative; it applies also to an unordained renunciant; or, in the case of <s>bhikṣuṇīs</s>, to a person from that same group. (240) One should not allow entry here for one who is not trustworthy. 'Here' means in the bathhouse. Even of one arriving at midday — this is another purpose for the doorkeeper. (241) Co-residents (<s>sārdhavihārin</s>) and pupils (<s>antevāsika</s>) should perform attendant duties here. 'Here' means in the bathhouse. (242) 'By juniors' — or 'by others' — this shows an alternative view. For some, an alternative reading: 'juniors should perform attendant duties in the bathhouse.' To show the form of the attendant duties, he says: (243-244) The provision of a lamp-pan, oil, tooth-sticks, cow-dung [cakes], clay-powder, drinking water, and so forth; the inspection of firewood; rubbing [the body]; bathing with oil; sweeping; removal of refuse, and so forth. The performing of attendant duties mutually among them. Thus the mutual performance of attendant duties such as rubbing and so forth among co-residents and pupils. (245) After cleaning the stool and the oyster-shell [scraper], placing them in their proper spot. The attendant duties referred to by the word 'and so forth' [are found] in the summary matrix [beginning with] 'this and so forth, standing in front, [up to] "should rub."' (246) Everywhere, this is the procedure for utensils. 'This' refers to 'after cleaning, placing in the proper spot.' (247) All equipment should be stored in a well-protected place. [The rule means] there is no equipment that is not to be stored — except for that within the bathhouse. This <s>sūtra</s> is for the purpose of regulation. (248) One should enter here with little noise. In the bathhouse. (249-250) Inspiring confidence; well-restrained in deportment (<s>īryāpatha</s>); self-aware (<s>saṃprajāna</s>). 'Well-restrained' shows non-distraction in body and speech by the quality of being well-restrained. 'Self-aware' shows [non-distraction] of mind. The quality of inspiring confidence in deportment is shown through these two modes. (251) One should not rub [another's body] by standing in front. One should not rub oneself by interposing [before] another who is rubbing — this is the meaning. (252) The avoidance of socializing (<s>saṃgaṇikā</s>). 'Here' continues [from the previous sūtra]; having entered the bathhouse in accordance with desires — since 'socializing is an inflamer of desires,' therefore its avoidance here is especially [enjoined]. (253) Reliance on noble silence (<s>āryatūṣṇībhāva</s>). 'Here' connects [with the previous]. This <s>sūtra</s> is for the purpose of averting unwholesome imaginings and mental states consonant with them. Bringing to the forefront proper attention (<s>yoniśomanasikāra</s>) should be understood as noble silence. (254) The taking of a triple staff (<s>tridaṇḍaka</s>) when going [somewhere]. At the time of going. (255) One should not perform attendant duties wearing only a single garment. Some interpret 'bathhouse' here as a reference to the body — mutual [rubbing] as explained in relation to the body. [The rule means] <s>bhikṣus</s> wearing only one garment should not perform mutual attendant duties in the bathhouse. [But the rule applies] everywhere in attendant duties, not only those related to the body, and in every place,

children.translated_text: The established nature of this rule is not [limited] to the steam-room alone; therefore it is not dependent on that. // (256) One should not have a faithless person perform this bodily [service]. // 'This' refers to personal care (<s>parikarma</s>); [merely] external work such as carrying loads and the like is not prohibited. // (257) Unwavering faith is intended here and in the preceding [rule]. // 'Unwavering' (<s>anitvarā</s>) means that which is unshakeable, having arisen over a long time. 'Here' refers to the subsequent rule on personal care. 'And in the preceding' refers to [the rule] 'one should not grant entry here to one without faith.' 'Intended' means what is meant. // (258) One equal to a lion should not attend upon one equal to a jackal. // The meaning is: one who is virtuous should not perform attendance upon one who is immoral. An exception to this is made: // (259-260) One should attend upon a teacher (<s>ācārya</s>) and preceptor (<s>upādhyāya</s>) who are extremely immoral, // and also sick parents, even if they are lay persons. // This permission is given because these [persons] are supremely beneficent. // (261) Bathing with a medicinal bath (<s>saṃbhāraka-snātra</s>). // [For the sick.] Here the narrative occasion is recited. The word 'sick' was not used in the formal enactment, [nor is there] impropriety of [bathing] for another [person] elsewhere. Since no specific [restriction] is adopted, it is connected with [the rule applying to] all. To illustrate its nature, [the sūtra] states: // (262) A bath with a decoction of wind-dispelling roots, tumors [i.e., tubers], leaves, flowers, and fruits — that is called [a medicinal bath]. // The meaning is: it is called a <s>saṃbhāraka-snātra</s> (bath with ingredients). // 'Nourishment' is the purpose in bathing. Thus these are the components [of such a bath]. How should one bathe? [The sūtra] states: // (263-264) Oil-application is for the purpose of preventing dryness. // With a secondary bath, for the removal of that [oil]. // The meaning is: the oil-application (<s>abhyakṣā</s>), consisting of anointing with oil and the like for the purpose of preventing dryness, [is removed] by means of a secondary bath (<s>upasnānaka</s>). // (265) In the final water-pot, two or three drops of oil should be given [for the earlier purpose]. // 'For the earlier purpose' means for preventing dryness. The meaning is: two or three drops of oil should be placed in the final water-pot. // (266) One should bathe in an iron tub. // The sick person should keep it. // 'It' refers to the iron tub. Keeping it by one who is not sick is not appropriate — nor should it be used like a lump of iron; this should be understood. Restlessness and the like — performing such things without purpose — all of that is understood to be a transgression (<s>duṣkṛta</s>), hence it was not [separately] stated in the sūtra. // (267) One should place a cover over it. // For the purpose of preventing the hot water from becoming cold. // (268) And here, a cushion-support (<s>gaṇḍopadhānikā</s>) for the neck. // 'Should give' continues [from above]. Bathing here should be without delay, so as not to cause discomfort. Therefore this [cushion] is given. // (269) One should not wash the feet just anywhere. // This pertains to the monastery. // (270) The place for this is at the drainage outlet (<s>pranāḍīmukha</s>). // 'This' refers to foot-washing. The textual passage is: The Blessed One said, 'One should wash at the drainage outlet.' // (271) They should have a foot-washing [basin] made. // Since the purpose is accomplished at the drainage outlet and the like even without this, [its use] is by the injunction [alone]. Therefore there is freedom of choice here, not a fixed rule — to show this, the verb is used at the beginning. A communal item is the place for this. And since one individual should not have a claim on communal property, the plural is used. In which location? [The sūtra] states: // (272) At the upper northeast corner of the monastery. // What is its shape? — (273) Work-tool shaped, rough. // Removal of dirt is the purpose here. // (274) One should set up a receptacle (<s>kaṭhilla</s>). // This is the name of the receiving vessel. Of what material?

children.translated_text: [The sūtra] states: made of clay. Gold, silver, <s>vaiḍūrya</s> (beryl), or crystal receptacles should not be set up; rather, [one] made of clay — this is the textual passage. What is its shape? — // (275) With an elephant-foot base, having a knob (<s>karṇikā</s>). // Non-rolling is the purpose here. The making of it with a knob is for the purpose of providing a foothold while washing the feet. Where is the knob placed so that [the basin] has one? [The sūtra] states: // (276) Placed in the middle. // Of what shape? [The sūtra] states: // (277) <s>Kadamba</s>-flower shaped and rough. // The roughness is for the purpose of preventing the feet from slipping. // (278) After washing, it should be stored upside down. // This washing is for the sake of making it presentable. Presentability means cleanliness. And whatever dirty water remains in it [must be removed]. Therefore it is not proper [to leave it]; thus one should [wash it] with other water — this should be understood. The textual passage is: 'Having washed the feet, one should discard the foot-water outside the monastery or at the drainage outlet, then wash [the basin] again.' Where should it be stored? [The sūtra] states: // (279-282) On top of a shelf, in the case of [a basin belonging to] the community. // For a personal one, at the door-frame of the cell. // The place in the monastery where one performs bowl-cleaning and the like — its cleaning with water or smearing — // [should be done] in the shape of a <s>kuntaphala</s> (pointed fruit) or a drum. // 'In the shape of' continues [from above]. With what should one smear? [The sūtra] states: // (283) With cow-dung or clay. // [Thus it is stated.] // (284) There is no fixed rule for the shape of the smearing when [the purpose is merely] valued substance [preservation]. // (285-287) One who is without a bowl should not be ordained or given full ordination. // Not with one that is deficient, excessive, or discolored. // There are three [sizes of] bowls: large, medium, and small. // To ascertain their measurements, [the sūtra] states: // (288) With the remainder [of space] above [the contents], up to the end of the upper portion, next to the thumb-belly [i.e., the fleshy part of the thumb], one <s>prastha</s> (a measure) of cooked rice or more, [or] twice that [amount] of <s>Māgadhaka</s> [measure], carrying [food] with <s>sūpa</s> (broth) and condiments — this is the medium [bowl]. [This is the standard.] // [Only] of the upper portion, not the lower. 'From the end, not from any other spot, the next [measure is] that of the thumb-belly' — at the joint-area, the breadth of the thumb, that much. With the remaining lower [portion of space], one <s>prastha</s> or more of cooked rice of the <s>Māgadhaka</s> [standard], or twice that upward — however much [the bowl] carries together with appropriate condiments, that is the proper and suitable [capacity] — this is the meaning. For liquids such as oil, ghee, honey, and water, thirty-two <s>palas</s> constitute one <s>Māgadhaka prastha</s>. For other non-liquid items, sixteen [<s>palas</s>] — these indicate the measure of the substance. // Therefore, it should be understood that the sixteen <s>palas</s> here are designated by the <s>Māgadhaka prastha</s>. // The textual passage [states]: 'Where two <s>Māgadhaka prasthas</s> of cooked rice with broth and condiments are placed and the thumb-belly does not touch the rim — that is the large [bowl]. Where one [<s>prastha</s> suffices] — that is the small. In between is the medium.' // Since broth and condiments are mentioned here for the purpose of [providing] flavor, the broth and condiments are proportionally factored in for moistening — therefore, when there are multiple types of condiments, they are proportionally factored in here. The amount of condiment that flavors the food — that much condiment is to be included in the bowl-measurement, and not more — this is the meaning. // To dispel the confusion of inferior, medium, and superior [standards] due to regional variation in the <s>pala</s> [measure], the authoritative measurement transmitted by tradition is stated: 'A <s>māṣa</s> is known to equal eight <s>raktikas</s>. A <s>tola</s> is declared to be eight <s>māṣas</s>.' A <s>tola</s>

children.translated_text: they call it gold; but a <s>pala</s> is [the weight of] eight gold pieces. (289) A <s>bhikṣuṇī</s> (nun) should not keep [a bowl] larger than the smallest [size] for <s>bhikṣus</s> (monks). What is the smallest for <s>bhikṣus</s> is the largest for her. The smallest for her is the practice of obtaining alms-food (<s>piṇḍapāta</s>) sufficient for a bowl-measure. (290) A disc of tin (<s>trapumaṇḍalaka</s>) is to be given by her at the base of the bowl. 'By her' means by the <s>bhikṣuṇī</s>. 'Here' means on the bowl. The 'base' (<s>niṣāda</s>) is that part by which the bowl stands on the ground; 'there' is the meaning. What is its shape? He says: (291) Of the shape of a <s>Bodhi</s>-fig leaf or the palm of the hand, (292) and also the measure. Not only in shape but also in measure, just this much should be given—no more, for exceeding the purpose [would be wrong]. The meaning is: for the attainment of stability. For contact with the ground, attaching a ring (<s>koṭaka</s>) is the purpose of this gift. (293) [The bowl] becomes genuine even if borrowed. 'Genuine' (<s>satattva</s>) means the state of having a bowl even if borrowed. With a borrowed [bowl], one should not ordain or give full ordination to one without a bowl. 'One should not be without a bowl during the rains'—such [rules] would be transgressed; this is the purpose of this [provision]. (294) Likewise the set of five. The three robes (<s>tricīvara</s>), the sitting-mat (<s>niṣadana</s>), and the water-strainer (<s>pariśrāvaṇa</s>)—just as with the bowl, so these too become genuine [even if borrowed]—this is the meaning. 'Therefore I permit: one should ordain even with six requisites (<s>pariṣkāra</s>) that are borrowed'—this is the text. Without a water-strainer and sitting-mat too, one should not ordain—this is the triad. From this, the [implication] should be understood. (295-296-297) One should not be without a bowl during the rains (<s>varṣā</s>). One should not go on a countryside journey. One may travel in dangerous situations with a damaged bowl. '<s>Upananda</s> ordained one without a bowl. He, traveling on a countryside journey together with <s>bhikṣus</s>, arrived at a market town. There, a householder invited the <s>bhikṣus</s> for a meal. Since that newly ordained one had no bowl, the householder was displeased. The Blessed One said: A <s>bhikṣu</s> should not travel the countryside without a bowl. [When bowls are] stolen by thieves, the Blessed One said: A damaged bowl should be carried, the [good] bowl should be stored, and during the rains the bowl should be presented'—this is the text. (298-299-300) One should not ordain [anyone] in [the bowl's] absence. One who has risen should not drag, throw, or dry the bowl. One should use it with moderation. To show its proper use, he says: (301) One should not cast off [food] into another [vessel] from this. 'Another' means a different vessel. 'Cast off' means in the manner of discarding. (302) One should not clean refuse with this [bowl]. 'One should not clean dregs' is the continuation. (303-308) One should not give hand- and mouth-washing water [in it]. One should not have it cleaned by a <s>śrāmaṇera</s> (novice) who is given to carelessness. Not with sand or cow-dung. One should not put it away too wet. One should not neglect it when too dry. One should not place it on stone. This placement is temporary. (309) Not in an impure place. (310) Not just anywhere. 'Place' is the continuation, as well as 'placement.' (311) One should not throw it down [carelessly]. This prohibition is for the purpose of [preventing] bending [the bowl] anywhere, not for that particular time. (312) A niche (<s>mālaka</s>) is to be made for this purpose. For the purpose of placing the bowl. '<s>Mālaka</s>' is the name for a window-niche (<s>gavākṣaka</s>). How is it to be made? He says: (313) For a monastery and its surrounding area that are being built, not by cutting the wall. (314) A <s>cakoraka</s> (basket-holder) by forest-dwelling [monks]. For the purpose of placing the bowl.

children.translated_text: By a variant reading of '<s>ākāśamālaka</s>' (open-air niche), this is the usage. Of what material? He says: (315) Made of creepers or of rope. The lid too should be made of creeper or rope, coated with cow-dung and clay—this is the meaning. (318-319-320) Hanging this on a tree with a strap is good in the wilderness. Not placement on the ground. One should not take it elsewhere. This is the <s>cakoraka</s> (basket-holder). (321) One should carry [the bowl] placed in a bag (<s>sthavikā</s>). (322) One should not carry it by hand. (323) In the armpit. Of the bowl, (324) carrying [is done] by providing a strap (<s>ālayanaka</s>). (325) One should place the bowl, medicine, and implements in separate bags. In one bag the bowl, in another medicine, in another the implements—this is the meaning. 'Implements' (<s>kolāhala</s>) means items such as awl, cord, etc. (326) One should maintain these. That is, the bags for the bowl etc. (327) One should not use straps of equal suspension for these bags. In these bags for bowl etc., straps of equal suspension should not be given—this is the meaning. And thus the narrative: 'Venerable one, is this a drum?'—such was the occasion. Therefore this is directed at prohibiting the use of equal suspension. (328) And narrow [bags] are difficult to get [things] out of. One should not use the arrangement of straps—for what reason? He says: they are difficult to get [things] out of. (329) For preventing contraction, the recommended [length] should not be given. In what area should the recommended [length] not be given? He says: (330) In the middle. [This refers to] the strap, as understood from the context. In the middle of the separate [bags], not of the long [strap]—this is to be understood from the meaning. (331) For its standing, giving a crow's-foot [fastener] at the intervals. (332-335) One should guard the bowl like one's eye. The <s>saṃghāṭī</s> (outer robe) like one's skin. And the remaining robes. One should not neglect their repair. Binding, firing, washing, sprinkling, and dyeing—for this statement pertains to both bowl and robe. (336) One should carry out bowl-repair in a secluded place. This <s>sūtra</s> is for the purpose of making known that this [repair work] when done in an unsecluded [place] is a cause of displeasure. (337-338) The <s>saṃgha</s> should appoint a blacksmith's tool-kit. For a crack—that [is to say], mending. (339) But it is not good [to mend] with molasses, lac, beeswax, tin, or lead. With what then is it good? He says: (340) Good [to mend] with strips, pegs, patches, and crocodile-tooth [clamps]. (341) And with powder of iron or stone. 'Good for mending' is the continuation. (342) Rubbing with oil. With the powder. How much? He says: (343) Until it resembles beeswax. With what is the rubbing [done]? He says: (344) With iron or <s>kuruvinda</s> (corundum). The meaning is: moistening the powder with oil, rubbing until it becomes like beeswax. (345) Applying in heat. Bowl—this is understood from the context. And that powder applied to the bowl— (346) Wrapping with wool (?), smearing with clay, and applying fire. This is the continuation. What kind of fire? He says: moderate.

children.translated_text: even afterward, more than two months. 'Afterward' is the key term. The word 'also' (<s>api</s>) serves to counter-prohibit [the view] that 'when there is no shelter (<s>niśraya</s>), one need not be guarded for more than two months.' It should be understood here that even without taking shelter for two months, one must act as a dependent. (379) They should examine him through exemptions relating to residence, acts, and those who maintain [him]. 'Thus' (<s>evam</s>) means residence (<s>vastu</s>); by exemptions relating to residence and so forth, they should examine this residence. 'Residence-exemption' means exemption in the shelter-dwelling. Because in a <s>saṃgha</s> eligible for shelter there is an abundance of persons, they should examine — enough with elaboration. (380) When there is an absence [of a shelter-giver] among the juniors, one should ask the most senior. 'Absence' refers to [the absence] of shelter. When the statement 'without shelter during the rains-retreat' has been made, among those who have taken shelter, one who has passed one year, having exceeded the teacher's period, who has gone to the <s>vihāra</s> without taking shelter due to a break in the rains — even non-shelter in the <s>vihāra</s> should not be done; if done, it constitutes a transgression (<s>sātisāra</s>). And the one among them who is the most senior — he should be asked. Immediately thereafter, the one who has been invited (<s>pravārita</s>) should perform the teacher-exemption. This is included in the stated text. In substance, the most senior among them is [relatively] junior — he is the dependent. The most senior therein is requested by the junior — this should be understood as 'dependent without certainty.' (381) Even when [a shelter-giver] is present, [one may take shelter] in the capacity of sub-dependence (<s>upaniśraya</s>). Thus, regarding shelter: even when the shelter-giver is present, at [his] shelter. Among juniors, the most senior should be asked. Here the text [states]: 'In the capacity of sub-dependence, this one becomes equal to the preceptor. This one alone should be asked by him. This one alone becomes his instructor; the one who recites also becomes a teacher' — thus it is stated in the section on construction in the <s>Pravrajyāvastu</s>. (382) One should not perform attendant service for one of another sect (<s>tajjātīya</s>) without examining [him], nor [allow] one of another sect to [serve] oneself. Here, 'one of another sect' means one ordained in another <s>nikāya</s> (school), whether known or suspected [to be so]. (383) It is faultless, when there is an absence [of one eligible for shelter], for one who has set out in search [of a shelter-giver], or even for one without shelter. 'Faultless' means without reproach. 'Absence' means of shelter. [The question] 'in what circumstance is it without reproach?' — for that purpose 'one who has set out in search' and so forth is stated. [The question] 'for how long?' — (384) Up to the conclusion of five nights. Thus it is stated. The meaning is: up to the limit of five nights. For the duration of five nights constitutes 'worthiness of obtaining.' Here the text from the origin [story states]: '<s>Upāli</s>, [to] a place without shelter,' up to 'having gone and examined, taking [it] from five nights.' (385) And worthiness [comes] in obtaining. Thus it is stated. And this is in the case of unobstructed connection and the search for shelter. (386-387) Having rested, a visiting [monk] should take shelter on the second or third day. Not for the sake of a single day. Thus 'he should take shelter' has the connection. (388) In the absence of the dependent, one should ask another [shelter-giver]. One who has performed the act of dependence is 'dependent' (<s>niśrita</s>). This is the <s>karmaṇi kta</s> (passive past participle formation) in the sense of 'taking shelter' — this is the meaning. (389) It is faultless for one who has gone for the sake of performing acts, upon the arrival of another [act] — when he has not been asked. For one who has gone for the purpose of performing acts, upon the arrival of another act to be performed, the absence of fault when he has not been asked — this is the meaning. This is from the <s>Vibhaṅga</s>, from the training rule on lodgings. 'He should take shelter' continues. [(390) Not from one whose [relationship is that] of his own.] (391) Having ascertained [his] conduct, knowledge, retinue, and capacity to support — through questioning and so forth — the acceptance of this [shelter-giver]. The conduct, knowledge, retinue, and supportive capacity — and his being engaged in reproof and so forth — of this person, having ascertained through questioning or by other means of behavior,
[VinSū 41]
